title: Designing a Simulation Study
text:
Why Simulate?
Analytic derivations can tell us the large-sample properties of an estimator, but they rarely tell us how that estimator behaves at a realistic sample size, under model misspecification, or when we have to deal with multiple nuisance models (e.g., propensity score, missing data, measurement error correction). Monte Carlo simulation fills that gap: we specify a data-generating mechanism (DGM) for which we know the truth, generate many random samples from it, apply the method(s) we want to evaluate, and compare the results back to the known truth.
Simulation is useful whenever you need to:

Model real-world random error and sampling variability
Approximate a quantity that is hard or impossible to solve for analytically
Test how well an estimator performs (bias, variance, confidence interval coverage) under known conditions
Understand what happens when an assumption is violated (e.g., unmeasured confounding)



The ADEMP Framework
Throughout this workshop we plan every simulation study using the ADEMP framework Morris, White, and Crowther, Statistics in Medicine, 2019, which organizes the design of a simulation study into five components:








Letter
Component
Question it answers




A
Aims
What are we trying to find out?


D
Data-generating mechanisms
How will we simulate data that reflects the scenario of interest?


E
Estimand
What quantity, exactly, are we trying to estimate?


M
Methods
Which estimator(s) will we apply to the simulated data?


P
Performance measures
How will we judge whether a method worked well?





The Running Example
Clinical question: Does taking prenatal vitamins during pregnancy reduce the risk of preterm birth?
The complication: We’re worried about confounding by maternal smoking. Smoking is associated with lower use of prenatal vitamins and a higher risk of preterm birth.









Mapped onto ADEMP, the running example looks like this:

Aims —


Quantify the bias in the estimated effect of prenatal vitamins on preterm birth when maternal smoking confounds the relationship but is unaccounted for in the analysis.
Compare approaches (naive, robust) to standard error estimation.
(Bonus): Planning sample size or understanding precision at a fixed sample size.


Data-generating mechanism — Simulate smoking status, both potential outcomes for preterm birth (with and without vitamins), observed vitamin use conditional on smoking, and the observed outcome — see Activity 1.
Estimand — The marginal risk difference, \(E[Y^{x=1}] - E[Y^{x=0}]\): the risk of preterm birth had everyone taken prenatal vitamins vs. had no one taken them.
Methods — An unadjusted risk difference, and inverse probability of treatment weighted (IPTW) risk differences using the known treatment weights — see Activities 1–2.
Performance measures — Bias (Activity 1), and average model-based vs. sandwich standard errors (Activity 2).

title: Activity 3
text:
Step 1. Outline the specific aims.
Context: We are planning a study of the effect of prenatal vitamin supplementation on the risk of preterm birth, worried about confounding by maternal smoking (unmeasured in our planned data source). Before we commit to a data source and sample size, we want to understand how sample size shapes what our study can tell us.
Simulation Objectives:

Assuming our hypothesized risk difference is correct, quantify how precision (ASE from both model-based and sandwich standard errors, and ESE) and the proportion of studies whose confidence interval would show a clear difference (power) change across a range of candidate sample sizes.
Turning that question around: at a couple of fixed, realistic sample sizes (as we might encounter with an existing registry or claims database), quantify the smallest effect size we could realistically detect.

text:
Step 2. Determine the appropriate data generating mechanism.

Helper functions
First, create the “helper” functions we will use throughout our simulation.








Function for DGM
This is the same DGM from Activities 1–2.








Set the seed
ALWAYS before any random number generation!








The hypothesized effect
Study planning mainly before we have data, so instead of an empirical “truth” recovered from a huge dataset, we plug in our best guess (from prior literature, pilot data, or clinical judgment) for each DGM parameter. We can still generate one very large sample under those hypothesized parameters just to confirm what marginal risk difference they imply.






The local (downloads) version uses a 10,000,000-person sample for the truth. Here in the browser we use 2,000,000 — still large enough for a very precise Monte Carlo estimate, but much faster to generate in webR.

title: Activity 3
section: Step 3. Define the estimand of the analysis.
text:
Step 3. Define the estimand of the analysis.
As in Activities 1–2, our estimand is the marginal risk difference, \(E[Y^{x=1}] - E[Y^{x=0}]\): the risk of preterm birth had everyone in the target population taken prenatal vitamins vs. had no one taken them.

title: Activity 3
section: Step 4. Identify the methods to be implemented in the study.
text:
Step 4. Identify the methods to be implemented in the study.
We will estimate the IPT-weighted risk difference (known weights), exactly as in Activity 2. Alongside the model-based standard error, we’ll also compute the robust sandwich standard error, which accounts for the fact that we’re using weights.

title: Activity 3
text:
Step 5. Specify the performance measures.
Precision. As in Activity 2, we’ll track a few measures of how precisely we can pin down the risk difference:

ASE, model-based: the average, across simulated samples, of the model-based standard error reported by the regression — what our software tells us about precision in a typical single sample.
ASE, sandwich: the same idea, but averaging the robust sandwich standard error instead.
ESE (empirical standard error): the standard deviation of the estimated risk differences across simulated samples — how much the estimate actually bounces around from sample to sample. If an ASE is close to the ESE, that standard error is trustworthy.

Power. Here we define power simply in terms of the confidence interval: the proportion of simulated samples whose 95% confidence interval (built from the model-based standard error) for the risk difference excludes zero (the value that would mean “no difference”).
\[Power \approx P\Big(0 \notin \big[\widehat{RD} - 1.96\times\widehat{SE}(\widehat{RD}),\; \widehat{RD} + 1.96\times\widehat{SE}(\widehat{RD})\big]\Big)\]
In other words: if our hypothesized effect is real, in what proportion of studies of this size would the confidence interval actually show a clear difference, rather than being consistent with “no effect”?

Simulating across a range of sample sizes

Function to simulate one sample-size scenario
This function draws nsim replicate samples at a given n, fits the IPTW model to each, and returns the estimated risk difference, its model-based and sandwich standard errors, and whether the model-based 95% CI excludes zero — for every replicate.








Run this across a grid of candidate sample sizes






The local (downloads) version sweeps N up to 40,000, with 300 replicates at each value. Here in the browser we use a smaller grid (up to N = 8,000) with 100 replicates, so the qualitative pattern is still visible but runs quickly.











How does N affect precision (ASE, sandwich ASE, and ESE)?








How does N affect power?

title: Activity 3
section: What effect could I detect with the data I have?
text:
What effect could I detect with the data I have?
So far we’ve asked: “given a hypothesized effect, how big a sample do I need?” But in pharmacoepidemiology we’re typically using an existing data source (an insurance claims database, a disease registry). The useful planning question becomes: “given the N in this data source (and my design choices), what’s the smallest effect I could realistically detect?”
We can answer this with the exact same simulation machinery, just swapping which quantity is fixed and which one varies.
Instead of looping over N at one hypothesized effect, we now fix N and loop over a grid of hypothesized effect sizes. We can also change the confounding parameters to see how that impacts our precision.

Function to simulate one effect-size scenario






We use the sandwich standard error directly here, since we know it more accurately estimates the empirical standard error.


Translating a hypothesized risk difference into the DGM
Our DGM generates the treatment effect on the log-odds scale (or_prenatal), but the effect we actually want to hypothesize about is the marginal risk difference. So first we write down, analytically, the exact marginal risk difference implied by a given or_prenatal (no simulation noise, since smoke only takes two values), then invert that numerically to find the or_prenatal that produces whatever risk difference we want to hypothesize.








Run this across a grid of hypothesized effect sizes, at a couple of fixed sample sizes






The local (downloads) version compares N = 1,000 vs. N = 10,000, with 250 replicates at each of 6 hypothesized risk differences. Here in the browser we compare N = 1,000 vs. N = 4,000, with 100 replicates at each.











Plot: power vs. hypothesized effect size, by sample size








The minimum detectable effect size, at each N

title: Activity 1
text:
Step 1. Outline the specific aims.
Context: We want to estimate the effect of prenatal vitamin supplementation on the risk of preterm birth. However, we are worried about confounding by maternal smoking, which is not measured in our data.
Simulation Objective: Quantify the magnitude and direction of bias in our estimate of the effect of prenatal vitamins on the risk of preterm birth under scenarios where maternal smoking decreases the use of prenatal vitamins but increases the risk of preterm birth.

title: Activity 1
text:
Step 2. The DGM.
We need to develop code that can generate one randomly sampled cohort based on our predefined data generating mechanism. We start with one cohort to build out this code.

Pseudo random number generation
1. Why do we want random numbers?
Simulations use random numbers to stand in for uncertainty / variability. We can use this to:

model real-world random error
approximate things that are hard to solve analytically

can’t use exact math? simulate!
we do this when want to know the “truth”

test statistical methods

see how well a test or estimator performs (bias, standard error, coverage)

bootstrap!

uses random resampling to estimate uncertainty


2. How does R generate random numbers?
Computers can’t generate truly random numbers. R uses a “pseudo-random number generator” — an algorithm that produces a seemingly random sequence of numbers but is fully determined by a starting value (the “seed”). The generator will not repeat for a long time, and for our purposes is random enough.
3. What are we doing when we set the seed?
When we set the seed, we are telling R where to start in the pseudo-random number sequence. This allows us to replicate our results in other R sessions. If we don’t set the seed, the pseudo-RNG uses the system clock and process ID, so results will differ every session.
4. Why do we care about setting the seed?
For reproducibility!






Now let’s set the seed for the rest of the simulation. Do this before any random number generation.








Assign our simulation parameters
Next, we set our simulation parameters based on the prenatal example. Setting them up as variables lets us change them easily and sets us up for success for creating a function later on.
Recall our DAG:













Create the simulated dataset using simulation parameters
We do this using potential outcomes. The steps are as follows:

Generate the baseline population, where 20% of the population are smokers.

\[Z\sim Bernoulli(p=0.2)\]

Next, generate the potential outcomes. For each individual, we generate the potential outcome for preterm birth under each “treatment strategy” (prenatal vitamins vs. no prenatal vitamins) conditional on smoking status. This allows us to recover the truth, because it breaks the confounding structure.

\[Y^{x=0}\sim~Bernoulli(p=expit(-2.33 +log(3)\times Z))\]
\[Y^{x=1}\sim~Bernoulli(p=expit(-2.33 +log(3)\times Z + log(0.9)\times X))\]

Generate observed treatment conditional on smoking status.

\[X|Z=1\sim Bernoulli(p=0.65)\]
\[X|Z=0\sim Bernoulli(p=0.85)\]

Assign the observed outcome based on the observed treatment.

\[Y = Y^{x=1}\times X + Y^{x=0}\times (1-X)\]








Aside: deriving the balancing intercept
Using R! Very helpful if we want to start moving parameters around and need to rederive the intercept.








Test the simulated dataset
Evaluate whether the marginal proportions of specific variables match your expectations.
Look at the marginal distribution of smoking. We would expect ~20% to have smoke equal to 1.






Look at the marginal distribution of prenatal vitamin supplementation. We would expect ~65% of smokers and ~85% of non-smokers to have prenatal equal to 1.






Look at the marginal probability of preterm birth. We would expect ~10% of the total population to have experienced a preterm birth.

title: Activity 1
section: Step 3. Define the estimand or target of the analysis.
text:
Step 3. Define the estimand or target of the analysis.
Here, we are interested in the total effect of prenatal vitamins on the risk of preterm birth. We want to quantify this as the marginal risk difference among the entire baseline population. Essentially, we want to contrast the risk had everyone received prenatal vitamins and the risk had no one received prenatal vitamins.
\[E(Y^{x=1})-E(Y^{x=0})\]

title: Activity 1
section: Step 4. Identify the methods to be implemented in the study.
text:
Step 4. Identify the methods to be implemented in the study.
We are not comparing methods but instead want to understand the effect of confounding on our results. As a result, we need only identify a method that targets the total effect of prenatal vitamin use on the risk of preterm birth. Direct outcome model adjustment would provide a conditional RD, while we want the marginal estimate that targets the baseline population.
One appropriate method for doing this is inverse probability of treatment weighting. Below, we calculate the unadjusted and adjusted RD.

Calculate the unadjusted risk difference.








Calculate the risk difference after adjusting for confounding by smoking.
First we estimate the weighted risk difference with the known weights.

With known weights for prenatal vitamins by smoking status






Here, we can see that the weighted risk difference is different from the unweighted estimate.

title: Activity 1
text:
Step 5. Specify the performance measures.
We have determined that we are interested in bias as a performance measure.
For each sample, bias is equivalent to \(\hat{\theta}-\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the true risk difference.
For multiple samples, \(Bias = E[\hat{\theta}] - \theta\). If we are only interested in bias, we don’t necessarily need to generate a bunch of repeated samples — we can just take one large sample and compare the unweighted and weighted estimates to the truth. Note this is not true for all scenarios: here our estimators converge to a true value as \(n\) grows large, are linear (risk difference), and we are not exploring issues with finite sample bias.
Using our large sample and potential outcomes we already generated, we can determine the “truth” to use for estimating bias. We could also do this mathematically, since this is a simple example — see the appendix of the slides.






If we have any interest in the sampling distribution of our estimators (MSE, variance, CI coverage), we need to move to repeated sampling. That’s what Activity 2 does next.

title: Activity 2
text:
Step 1. Outline the specific aims.
Context: We want to estimate the effect of prenatal vitamin supplementation on the risk of preterm birth. However, we are worried about confounding by maternal smoking, which is not measured in our data. We also want to understand the implications for different approaches to standard error estimation.
Simulation Objectives:

Quantify the magnitude and direction of bias in our estimate of the effect of prenatal vitamins on the risk of preterm birth under scenarios where maternal smoking decreases the use of prenatal vitamins but increases the risk of preterm birth (Activity 1).
Compare the 95% confidence interval coverage for the risk difference using different approaches to standard error estimation, including model-based SEs and sandwich SEs (Activity 2).

title: Activity 2
section: Step 2. Determine the appropriate data generating mechanism.
text:
Step 2. Determine the appropriate data generating mechanism.

Helper functions
First, create the “helper” functions we will use throughout our simulation.








Function for the DGM
Create a function for the DGM that we can randomly sample from. The code is near-identical to the code from the one-random-sample example in Activity 1, but adds in a derivation for the intercept so we can change parameters without having to re-derive it by hand each time.








Set the seed
ALWAYS before any random number generation!








Generate the “truth”
First, create a large re-sampled dataset from which to derive the truth. By doing this after setting the seed, we ensure that we use the same random state start and thus do not overlap with random states from the “observed” data. See Morris et al. (2019) for additional detail on this.






The local (downloads) version uses a 10,000,000-person sample for the truth. Here in the browser we use 2,000,000 — much faster to generate in webR.











Resample many times
Now we want to re-sample from this DGM many times to understand the sampling behavior of our estimators. Note that we are not resetting the seed with each iteration. See Morris et al. (2019) for additional detail.






The local (downloads) version uses 1,000 replicates. Here in the browser we use 500, which is enough to see the qualitative pattern in bias and coverage, though the estimates will look noisier.

title: Activity 2
section: Step 3. Define the estimand of the analysis.
text:
Step 3. Define the estimand of the analysis.
The slides illustrate how to derive the truth mathematically. However, this is sometimes challenging to do but can be estimated from the DGM with a large n. So, we illustrate how to do that below.

title: Activity 2
section: Step 4. Identify the methods to be implemented in the study.
text:
Step 4. Identify the methods to be implemented in the study.
We are comparing two estimators:

Unweighted risk difference
IPT weighted risk difference (known weights)

Within the weighted risk difference, we are further comparing two approaches for standard error estimation:

Model-based SEs
Sandwich estimator for SEs


Add IPT weights to the samples
We add the “known” treatment weight to each sample — known because we set the true treatment-assignment probabilities for the simulation. In a real observational study we wouldn’t know these; we’d have to estimate instead.








Sample-specific analysis
Within each sample, we want to estimate the unadjusted risk difference and the weighted risk difference and their associated model-based standard errors. Additionally, for the weighted risk difference we will estimate the robust sandwich standard errors to account for the weights.

title: Activity 2
text:
Step 5: Performance measures

Sample-specific set-up
To estimate bias and coverage, we need to do an additional data manipulation to the results from each simulation sample.
95% confidence interval coverage is the proportion of times the true risk difference is captured within the 95% confidence interval. Within each sample, we create a binary variable that is 1 if the confidence interval from that sample contains the true risk difference and 0 if it does not:
\[I(\hat{\theta}-1.96\times\hat{SE}(\hat{\theta}) \leq \theta \leq \hat{\theta}+1.96\times\hat{SE}(\hat{\theta}) )\]
where \(I( )\) is the indicator function (\(=1\) if expression in parenthesis is true, \(=0\) if false)
Bias is mean error across simulations. Within each sample, we calculate error as:
\[\hat{\theta}-\theta\]








Estimate performance measures
Summary statistics of the simulation-specific values we already estimated

title: Activity 2
text:
Plots
Below are some ideas for presenting simulation results.
Well, the first one is more just to get a feel for what the sampling distribution looks like.






The boxplot is a nice way to visualize bias and spread all in one figure. This shows bias and ESE – so doesn’t give a good sense of how the standard error estimators are doing.






Below shows how coverage is performing in each simulation. Unadjusted is doing the worst (the most red/pink), whereas the adjusted with robust SE is doing the best (the most blue).

title: Activity 2
text:
When things go wrong
If we have parameters close to the edge of the parameter space (e.g., rare exposure, rare outcome), we can run into issues with model convergence in some of the samples.
We can set up our simulation code defensively to collect when a simulation fails and keep going, rather than failing and stopping the program altogether.
For example, let’s make the comparator more rare (i.e., more people taking prenatal vitamins)






The local (downloads) version uses 1,000 replicates here too. Here in the browser we use 500 to keep things fast.









The simulation failed at the indexes printed above. We can now see why our simulation failed because we saved the error messages. When estimating our performance measures or calculating Monte-Carlo error, we will need to take into account that our actual number of successful simulations is smaller.

title: ISPE 2026 Simulation Workshop
text:
This workshop covers how to design, implement, and evaluate a Monte Carlo simulation study — using confounding by an unmeasured variable, inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), and standard error estimation as a running example.
Topics include:

The ADEMP framework (Aims, Data-generating mechanisms, Estimand, Methods, Performance measures) for planning a simulation study
Building a data-generating mechanism (DGM) from a causal diagram, and deriving a “balancing intercept” so the DGM matches a target marginal outcome risk
Scaling a single simulated sample up to thousands of replicates to study the sampling behavior of an estimator
Comparing standard error estimators (model-based vs. sandwich/robust) by their confidence interval coverage

The workshop alternates between didactic sessions and hands-on activities. This site hosts the activity materials. Each activity page contains live, runnable R code powered by webR — no local R installation needed. When you load an activity page, the necessary packages download automatically in the background. Once ready, click Run on any code block to execute it directly in your browser.
